entries.clue: New technology briefly shown by couple blowing cover (10,12)

annotation.definition: New technology briefly shown by couple blowing cover

blocks.clueFragment: New technology briefly shown by couple
blocks.note: the meant reading: shortened, this new technology is written with a couple of letters, the pair of capitals everyone now uses for it
the surface reading: a pair of spies whose cover story is blown, which pushes the reader towards espionage

annotation.surface: A pair of undercover agents exposed by some new gadget.
annotation.walkthrough: The spy story is the misdirection: the answer's second word is the spies' word for secret information, but here it means machine thinking, shortened to AI, a couple of letters.
annotation.definitionFit: Computer systems that learn, reason and write text are the headline technology of recent years, and the field is universally known by two capitals.

entries.clue: Large bird’s backside caught (4)

indicatorNotes.caught: to catch what someone says is to hear it, so what you catch is a sound

blocks.note: a rear is a backside; in southern British speech its final R is silent
sound indicator

annotation.surface: A remark about a big bird whose rear end has been grabbed.
annotation.walkthrough: The ’s stands for ‘is’, joining the bird to its wordplay. The match relies on a non-rhotic accent, where rear ends in a vowel.
annotation.definitionFit: This flightless South American runner stands well over a metre tall, a smaller cousin of the ostrich and emu.

entries.clue: Setter’s new tipple — beer infused with dash of cognac, very slight (13)

indicatorNotes.new: a new version of the letters is a rearranged one, a fresh mix
indicatorNotes.infused with: the C is steeped into the beer, so it joins the letters before they are mixed
indicatorNotes.dash of: a dash is a small splash of drink, here just the first letter

blocks.note: the setter is I, so setter's = I'M, I am
anagram fodder, rearranged by 'new'
first letter of cognac, mixed in with the fodder

annotation.surface: The setter describes a new drink: beer with a splash of brandy.
annotation.walkthrough: The ’s on Setter is a contraction, not a possessive: the setter is I, so it gives I'M. 'Infused with' tells you the C joins the beer before the shake-up.
annotation.definitionFit: Something too faint or small to be noticed at all is slight in the extreme, so the adjective swaps cleanly for the phrase.

entries.clue: Back in Scilly … divine, simply beautiful (7)

indicatorNotes.Back: going back means travelling in the opposite direction, so the letters are read in reverse
indicatorNotes.in: the letters sit inside the words that follow, not spread across the whole clue

blocks.note: the run starts after the S of Scilly and ends two letters into divine
indicators: hidden, then read in reverse

annotation.surface: A holiday postcard: back on the Isles of Scilly, divine, simply beautiful.
annotation.walkthrough: The Isles of Scilly are islands off Cornwall, a classic British holiday spot, so 'Back in Scilly' reads as a return trip. The ellipsis just bridges the gap between the two words the letters span.
annotation.definitionFit: The word describes an unspoilt, peaceful scene of pastoral charm, beauty of the plain and simple kind rather than grandeur.

entries.clue: Where Hatton Garden is turning over diamonds? (3)

indicatorNotes.turning over: a thing turned over is upside down, so a down entry's letters run bottom to top

blocks.note: Hatton Garden is in the London postcode EC1, with the 1 read as the letter I
reversal indicator: the postcode is read from the other end

annotation.surface: A question about where London's diamond quarter is doing its trading.
annotation.walkthrough: Hatton Garden is London's jewellery and diamond district, so the surface points at the trade; the wordplay needs its postcode, EC1, with 1 standing in for I.
annotation.definitionFit: Underworld slang calls gems, especially cut stones, by the name of frozen water because they sparkle clear and cold.

entries.clue: Where soldier goes right in, surrounded by deceased (7)

blocks.note: the late X = the deceased X; its letters wrap round the filling
R = right
the word itself, placed after R

annotation.surface: A grim battlefield picture: a soldier goes in among the dead.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Goes' in the definition means answers a call of nature, not advances. The word 'in' reads as part of the soldier's movement but gives its own letters here.
annotation.definitionFit: Army camps dig a communal toilet trench, so this is where a soldier relieves himself; 'goes' is the euphemism.

entries.clue: New unrestricted hangar section opened by airline in High Peak (5,6)

indicatorNotes.unrestricted: restrictions are the limits at the edges, so removing them strips the outer letters
indicatorNotes.opened by: the section is split open and the airline goes into the gap

blocks.note: N = new
hANGAr without its outer letters
a section is a part; it is split to take the airline
BA = British Airways, placed inside PART

annotation.surface: News of a new open-plan hangar, part of it taken over by an airline, up in the Peak District.
annotation.walkthrough: High Peak is a real district of Derbyshire in England, so the capitals disguise the definition as a place name. The answer is a Himalayan mountain in Pakistan, one of the world's highest.
annotation.definitionFit: This Himalayan summit in Pakistan rises above 8,000 metres, the ninth highest mountain on Earth.

entries.clue: Had to tidy without starter (5)

indicatorNotes.without starter: the starter is what comes first, so the word loses its opening letter

blocks.note: to neaten is to tidy
the six-letter verb loses its first letter, N

annotation.surface: Someone who had to tidy up, having skipped the first course.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Had' looks like the start of an obligation, 'had to'; it is the definition on its own, as in 'had a sandwich'. 'Starter' plays on the first course of a meal.
annotation.definitionFit: To have lunch is to consume it, so the past participle after 'have' works for a meal: 'I've had lunch'.

entries.clue: Canadian region’s golden underwear item in Franglais (8)

blocks.note: the French article la, the start of a half-French phrase
an English word dropped into the French
French d'or, 'of gold'; OR is gold in heraldry

annotation.surface: A gold bra, described in a mix of French and English, from somewhere in Canada.
annotation.walkthrough: Franglais is French mixed with English: 'la bra d'or' is a golden bra in a French that no French speaker would use. Canada is bilingual, which makes the surface plausible.
annotation.definitionFit: It is the mainland part of the province of Newfoundland and Labrador, a sparsely populated area on the Atlantic coast.

entries.clue: Hard work, reversing a long way in sports car (5)

far = a long way; reversed to RAF

annotation.surface: A struggle to back a sports car a long way.
annotation.walkthrough: The reversing sports car is the surface, but the reversing applies only to 'a long way'. The answer is British slang for hard work.
annotation.definitionFit: British informal usage has this word for toil or sustained effort, as in 'years of hard graft'.

entries.clue: Club’s dark blemish? (9)

blocks.note: night = the dark, as in 'after dark'
a spot is a blemish

annotation.surface: A golf club, perhaps, with an ugly dark mark on it.
annotation.walkthrough: The ’s reads as a possessive, but it is 'is', linking the definition to the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: A venue for drinking and dancing late in the evening is a nightclub, and this compound is an informal name for one.

anagram fodder, 18 letters

annotation.definitionFit: Radar networks that detect incoming missiles or aircraft give a military advance notice of attack, so they count as defence equipment.

entries.clue: Each penny invested in miniature table (6)

annotation.definitionFit: This is a small tripod stand from India, often used to hold a tea caddy, which suggests its folk link with tea.

entries.clue: Former colour rarely gone forever? (7)

blocks.note: ex = former
tinct is an archaic, rarely used word for a colour or tint

annotation.walkthrough: 'Rarely' is not a comment on the colour but a label on the word: TINCT is rare or old-fashioned for colour.
annotation.definitionFit: Said of a species like the dodo, it means no living members remain, which is to say it has vanished permanently.

entries.clue: Boastful character Humphrey stripped of Oscar for banter (8)

annotation.walkthrough: The Oscar looks like an Academy Award, which fits the actor; it is only the letter O.
annotation.definitionFit: A person who brags, blowing their own trumpet at every turn, is a plain synonym for a show-off.

anagram indicator

entries.clue: Might box contain these dark arts? (5,5)

the dark arts are sorcery used for evil

annotation.surface: A sinister question: could a box hold forbidden sorcery?
annotation.walkthrough: Black Magic is a long-running British assortment of dark chocolates sold in a box; the 'dark' of the dark arts also nods to the chocolate.
annotation.definitionFit: Sorcery used for evil ends is the dark arts, and Rowntree's boxed chocolate assortment carries the same name.

entries.clue: One of the 28 alternately at rest? Why yes (6)

annotation.definitionFit: In Greek myth she was a sea goddess, daughter of Uranus and Gaia, and so a member of that giant race of elder gods.

entries.clue: Doctor Roger testing a stool, possibly? (18)

entries.clue: Some trap a perch as escapist pursuit (5,5)

entries.clue: Case note drama that’s reviewed after the event (6,6)

entries.clue: Least tense, most impatient (9)

entries.clue: Concerning helpful light lit once more (9)

entries.clue: Perhaps Harris Tweed might be used to make this pilot’s clothing? (6,6)

entries.clue: Ignore parade ground command (4)

blocks.note: to ignore someone is to avoid or snub them
the barked, clipped form of 'Attention!' on the drill square

annotation.surface: A soldier told to disregard an order on the parade ground.
annotation.walkthrough: A drill sergeant shouts 'Atten-SHUN', clipped to its last syllable.
annotation.definitionFit: To avoid or snub someone deliberately is to ignore them, and the drill sergeant's clipped 'Attention!' gives the same word.

entries.clue: No end of appalling beer for one from Castle Combe? (8)

indicatorNotes.No end of: with no end, the word loses its final letter

blocks.note: VILE, appalling, without its last letter
lager is a beer

annotation.surface: A complaint about endless bad beer at a pub in a pretty village.
annotation.walkthrough: Castle Combe is a picture-postcard village in Wiltshire, England; the name suggests a castle rather than a village.
annotation.definitionFit: Castle Combe is a tiny Cotswold settlement, so a resident is defined by example as someone living there.

entries.clue: Welsh side extra gutted after pens? (7)

indicatorNotes.gutted: a gutted fish has its insides removed, so only the outer letters remain
indicatorNotes.after: after means following, so EA is placed behind SWANS

blocks.note: a pen is a female swan
ExtrA with its insides removed

annotation.surface: A Welsh football team gutted after losing in extra time on penalties.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is football: extra time, then 'pens', penalties. A pen is also a female swan, and the answer's club is nicknamed the Swans.
annotation.definitionFit: The city's football club plays in Wales's second city, and a side is a team.

entries.clue: Disaster Relief commercial covering India (3)

indicatorNotes.covering: a thing covering another lies around it, so AD goes round the I

blocks.note: an ad is a commercial; it covers I
I = India in the NATO alphabet

annotation.surface: A charity advertisement about India appealing for disaster relief.
annotation.walkthrough: The capitals make 'Disaster Relief' look like a charity's name; the answer is the ordinary word for such help, as in Band Aid.
annotation.definitionFit: Food, money and medicine sent to a stricken region is the ordinary word for humanitarian help after a catastrophe.

entries.clue: Burning to get off (6)

blocks.note: on fire, as in 'the barn was set ...'
what a passenger does leaving a bus or train

annotation.surface: Someone desperate to escape, or eager to get off.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Burning to' reads as 'longing to', joining the two halves into one wish; they are separate definitions.
annotation.definitionFit: The adjective means on fire, and the verb, formal for leaving a vehicle, means stepping down from it.

entries.clue: Sauce named after a bunch of keys? (8,6,8)

annotation.definition: Sauce named after a bunch of keys?

blocks.note: the surface reading: a sauce named after something ordinary
the meant reading: a key is a small low island, as in the Florida Keys, and this sauce is named after a large cluster of them

annotation.surface: A sauce, oddly, named after the keys on a key ring.
annotation.walkthrough: Keys look like the ones on a key ring; a key is also a small island or reef. The sauce takes its name from an archipelago in the St Lawrence River between Canada and the US.
annotation.definitionFit: The pink mayonnaise-and-ketchup salad sauce is named after an archipelago of some 1,800 isles in the St Lawrence River.
